rubric: PYTHON AS A FIRST LANGUAGE / BASICS / CHAPTER 2

slides.title: Variables and types
slides.main: The program learns to remember: a variable is a labeled box for a value.

items.title: Assignment
items.sub: Value on the right, box name on the left

body.text: In the last chapter every print command forgot everything at once. Today the program gets memory: the big step from calculator to program.

slides.title: Assignment
slides.main: The right side is evaluated first, then the result goes into the box.

body.text: age = 20

cells.title: age
cells.sub: Box name · where we put it

body.text: Read it not as “equals” but as “put”: into the box age, put twenty.

slides.title: Using a variable
slides.sub: A name is a reference to the current contents
slides.main: Put in a new value, and the old one vanishes without a trace.

body.text:
age = 20
print(age)    # 20
age = 21
print(age)    # 21 — the old one is gone
There is always exactly one value in the box: whoever asks about age gets what lies there now.

slides.title: Naming rules
slides.main: Age and age are two different boxes, a common source of half-hour debugging.

cells.title: 2user
cells.sub: Starting with a digit: not allowed

body.text:
Age = 20
age = 21      # two different boxes
Case matters: Python quietly creates two boxes and never warns you. Before blaming the logic, check the case.

slides.title: Naming style
slides.sub: In Python, snake_case is the norm
slides.main: Code is read ten times more often than it is written.

cells.title: user_count
cells.sub: Lowercase words with underscores: the name reads like a phrase

cells.title: x
cells.sub: Saves three seconds of typing, steals three minutes from the reader

body.text: Names should speak: a user counter is user_count, not a faceless x.

slides.title: Numbers: int and float
slides.sub: Whole for counting, fractional for measuring
slides.main: Values come in different kinds, and Python tells them apart.

body.text:
age = 20         # int — whole number
height = 1.76    # float — fractional, with a point

slides.title: Strings: str
slides.sub: Text in quotes, and its length
slides.main: A username and an email address are strings, not numbers.

body.text:
name = "Anna"
len(name)            # 4
len("Hello Anna")    # 10 — the space counts too
The len function returns the number of characters, spaces included.

slides.title: Logical type: bool
slides.sub: The answer to a closed question: yes or no
slides.main: Only two values: True and False, both capitalized.

body.text: is_adult = True
There is no third value. bool really comes into its own in the chapter on conditions, where the program starts to choose.

slides.title: The type function
slides.sub: Ask Python itself what kind a value is
slides.main: A useful habit when it is unclear whether you hold a number or a string that looks like one.

body.text:
type(20)      # int
type("20")    # str — looks alike, different cargo
It helps most when the value came from outside: a form, a file, a server response.

slides.title: f-strings
slides.sub: The main way to build text
slides.main: The letter f before the quotes, variable names in curly braces.

body.text:
age = 20
print(f"I am {age} years old")    # I am 20 years old

cells.title: f
cells.sub: A flag before the opening quote

body.text: A greeting with a name, a counter with a number, a report with totals: all easy with f-strings.

slides.title: Changing a variable
slides.sub: Old plus one, and back into the box
slides.main: This is how likes, steps and attempts are counted.

body.text:
count = count + 1    # old + 1 → back into the box
count += 1           # the same, shorter
Plus-equals reads as “add and put back”. Every new click on a heart is plus-equals in action.

slides.title: Type conversion
slides.sub: Converting a value to the kind we need
slides.main: Only like can be added: the string "5" plus the number 5 is a type error.

body.text:
int("42")     # 42 — string to number
str(42)       # "42" — number to string
"5" + 5       # TypeError: Python does not guess
The error is a gift here: the program crashes at once and loudly, instead of quietly computing nonsense.

slides.title: Summary
slides.main: The program learned to remember: the big step from calculator to program.
